first_impression.reaction: Googled 'greek orthodox wedding' expecting soft-focus photos and 'your dream day' copy. Instead the first lines are rules: it's a sacrament, two parts, no spoken vows, and 'sit down with your parish priest' before you book anything. A planning company telling me to see the priest before I see them? Fair enough. I went to the FAQ first, then the requirements and the Greece section. The rules are pinned to the Archdiocese, the OCA and Smartraveller, and there's a dated 'As at November 2026'. A couple of cultural asides aren't backed by anything, and one FAQ dodges a straight yes or no, but nothing here smells like a sales trick.

journey.quote: Before you hold a venue or send a save-the-date, sit down with your parish priest, check that the Church can marry you, and check that your date is open.
journey.reaction: They're telling me not to pay a deposit until the Church says yes. That's the opposite of an upsell. Noted.

journey.quote: When your priest has confirmed the Church side, [book a Wedded Concierge consultation](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=greek-orthodox-wedding&utm_content=primary) and plan the celebration around it.
journey.reaction: A booking link before the article has shown me anything. At least it's conditional on the priest, so it's not pushy. Still, evidence first, then the ask.

journey.section: Who can marry in the Greek Orthodox Church?
journey.quote: These are the rules for a Greek Orthodox wedding in Australia. For a wedding in Greece, the local Metropolis sets the requirements, so confirm them with your parish priest and the Metropolis.
journey.reaction: Names whose rules these are and admits they may differ in Greece. That's the kind of limit most sites skip.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: The non-Orthodox spouse does not become a member of the Church through the wedding and may not receive Holy Communion, and non-Orthodox clergy may not co-celebrate the service.
journey.reaction: The awkward bits stated plainly. If I were the non-Orthodox one, this is exactly what I'd want to know before the families start talking.

journey.section: Documents the parish usually asks for
journey.quote: They are often the slowest document to arrive.
journey.reaction: Probably true, but 'often' according to whom? It's advice dressed as fact. Minor.

journey.quote: Both are completed in the presence of the priest at least one calendar month before the wedding, and preferably three.
journey.reaction: Numbers and a deadline. Goes straight into my spreadsheet.

journey.quote: In many Greek families the wedding sponsor is expected to baptise the first child, so choose with both roles in mind.
journey.reaction: Useful if true, but 'many Greek families' is a generalisation with nothing behind it. I'd check it with the in-laws, not this page.

journey.section: Dates when weddings are not held
journey.quote: Easter falls on a different date each year, so confirm the calendar with your priest for your year before you hold any date.
journey.reaction: Concrete list of closed dates, plus an honest 'check your year'. Good.

journey.section: How long is a Greek Orthodox wedding?
journey.quote: The length depends on the parish, the priest and how much of the service is sung, so ask your priest for your church's running time.
journey.reaction: I'd have liked a ballpark, but I'd rather 'ask your priest' than a made-up number. They didn't pad it.

journey.section: Having a Greek Orthodox wedding in Greece
journey.quote: Many Greek-Australian families hope to marry on the island where a grandparent was baptised.
journey.reaction: Nice sentiment, no evidence. Reads like a brochure line in an otherwise factual section.

journey.quote: It charges the Metropolis fee on top of its package.
journey.reaction: That's the catch I go looking for, and they put it on the page themselves. Makes me believe the rest more.

journey.quote: Mykonos Grand states that both bride and groom must be Christian Orthodox to hold a religious wedding on the hotel premises.
journey.reaction: A venue rule that could kill a mixed-faith booking, flagged up front. Good.

journey.quote: Back home, you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but it is usually recognised if it was valid where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law.
journey.reaction: Dated, sourced to Smartraveller, and it tells me to get a lawyer to confirm. No pretending it's all handled.

journey.section: Can a Greek Orthodox wedding be held outside a church?
journey.quote: The rite takes place in church, before the Holy Altar.
journey.reaction: So is the answer no? It slides straight into resort chapels without saying 'no beach or garden ceremony'. Give me the yes or no first.

journey.section: Questions to ask the priest and the venue
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is a single point of contact who plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the service your priest confirms, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins;
journey.reaction: 'Fee agreed in writing' is the right signal. Still doesn't say whether venues pay you too, but that's a question for a call.

unanswered_questions: Can a Greek Orthodox wedding be held on a beach or in a garden, or is it church or chapel only? The FAQ implies no but doesn't say it.
Does Wedded Wonderland take a commission or mark-up from venues like Elounda or Nana Princess? (deferred business detail)
Is there a real Greek Orthodox wedding in Greece with the actual budget I can look at?
Roughly how long before the date do we need to start the Greece paperwork, end to end, given the three-month validity window and four-week approval?

turn_offs_found.quote: When your priest has confirmed the Church side, [book a Wedded Concierge consultation](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=greek-orthodox-wedding&utm_content=primary) and plan the celebration around it.
turn_offs_found.why: It's a CTA before any evidence. The wording is soft and conditional, so it's minor, but I want to see the proof before the ask.

turn_offs_found.quote: In many Greek families the wedding sponsor is expected to baptise the first child, so choose with both roles in mind.
turn_offs_found.why: A cultural generalisation with no source, sitting next to properly sourced Church rules. It blurs the line between rule and custom.

turn_offs_found.quote: Many Greek-Australian families hope to marry on the island where a grandparent was baptised.
turn_offs_found.why: Emotional scene-setting instead of facts. Harmless, but it's the tone I skip.

turn_offs_found.quote: The rite takes place in church, before the Holy Altar.
turn_offs_found.why: It answers a yes-or-no question sideways. When a page won't say 'no' plainly, I start wondering what it's avoiding.

would_share_with: My fiancee, the 'Who can marry' and 'Dates when weddings are not held' sections
Both sets of parents, the koumbaros section and the Greece paperwork steps

cta_reaction.why: The page earned some trust: it sends me to the priest first, names its sources, flags the Metropolis fee and the Mykonos Grand rule, and says the fee is agreed in writing. I'd still want to know whether venues pay them before I hand over details, but I'd take a call.

top_3_changes: Answer the FAQ 'Can a Greek Orthodox wedding be held outside a church?' with a plain yes or no first. 'The rite takes place in church, before the Holy Altar.' implies no but never says it; for example, lead with 'Not on a beach or in a garden: the service is held in a church or consecrated chapel.' (only if the source supports 'consecrated').

Mark custom as custom. 'In many Greek families the wedding sponsor is expected to baptise the first child' and 'They are often the slowest document to arrive.' read as facts but have nothing behind them; soften to 'is often expected' / 'can be slow', or attribute them.

Optional: move the primary CTA below 'Who can marry' so evidence comes before the ask, and trim 'Many Greek-Australian families hope to marry on the island where a grandparent was baptised.' to something checkable or cut it.

No invented brand facts; commission and real-budget questions placed in unanswered_questions as deferred

open_questions.question: Does the source pack support a plain 'no' to outdoor (beach or garden) Orthodox ceremonies? If so, the FAQ should lead with it.

assumptions: Daniel arrived via Google for 'greek orthodox wedding' while comparing three planners; a Greek Orthodox ceremony is in play for his wedding, so relevance is 4.
No prices are deliberate and not penalised.
